## memory:jaffle-data-coverage
Order data starts on 2022-09-19 (Philadelphia opened 2022-09-26), so 2022 is a partial year. The latest data is usually mid-month: check ordered_at:max before any "this month / this year / YTD" question. Treat the current month as incomplete (whole_periods_only: true). Compare year-to-date against the same calendar cut-off in the prior year, never against the full prior year. Stores that opened mid-period (e.g. Los Angeles, Oct 2025) have small samples; flag this when they top a ranking.

## memory:jaffle-same-store-growth
For any growth or year-over-year question at company level, report two numbers: the headline growth, and same-store growth. Same-store growth counts only stores open for the whole of both periods: filter stores.opened_at < the start of the earlier period. Store openings: Philadelphia Sep 2022, Brooklyn Apr 2023, Chicago May 2024, San Francisco Jun 2024, New Orleans Apr 2025, Los Angeles Oct 2025. Headline growth is driven mostly by new stores; same-store growth is the underlying health of the business. Example: 2025 vs 2024 net sales grew +69% headline but only about +4% same-store (Philadelphia + Brooklyn). Explain the gap by naming which stores opened or had their first full year.
Growth / YoY: always report headline AND same-store growth (stores open for both full periods)

## Learnings (3)

- **Mjaffle-data-coverage** (`demo_database.orders.ordered_at`): Order data starts on 2022-09-19 (Philadelphia opened 2022-09-26), so 2022 is a partial year. The latest data is usually mid-month: check ordered_at:max before any "this month / this year / YTD" question. Treat the current month as incomplete (whole_periods_only: true). Compare year-to-date against the same calendar cut-off in the prior year, never against the full prior year. Stores that opened mid-period (e.g. Los Angeles, Oct 2025) have small samples; flag this when they top a ranking.
- **Mjaffle-money-in-cents** (`demo_database.orders.order_total`, `demo_database.orders.subtotal`, `demo_database.orders.tax_paid`): Money is stored as **integer cents**. On `orders` the columns `subtotal`, `tax_paid`, and `order_total` are cents; so are `products.price` and `supplies.cost`. Do not `sum` these raw columns for a dollar figure. Use the `dollars` aggregation (`order_total:dollars`) or the pre-built dollar measures (`total_revenue`, `net_sales`, `tax_collected`, `avg_order_value`), which divide by 100.
- **Mjaffle-new-customers** (`demo_database.orders.customer`, `demo_database.orders.ordered_at`, `demo_database.orders.unique_customers`): A new customer in period P is a customer whose first-ever order (ordered_at:min per orders.customer) falls in P. This takes a two-stage query. Stage 1 (name it first_orders): source orders, dimensions [customer], measures [{name: first_order_at, formula: ordered_at:min}]. Stage 2: source first_orders, measures [*:count], filters first_order_at >= start of P and < end of P. Returning customers in P = unique_customers in P minus new customers in P. To count distinct buyers, always use the unique_customers measure (customer:count_distinct), not order rows.

WITH _base AS (
  SELECT
    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2025-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        AND orders.ordered_at < CAST('2025-10-30 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        THEN orders.subtotal
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) / 100.0 AS "orders.ly",
    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2026-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        AND orders.ordered_at < CAST('2026-10-30 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        THEN orders.subtotal
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) / 100.0 AS "orders.ty",
    SUM(
      CASE
        WHEN orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2026-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        AND orders.ordered_at < CAST('2026-10-30 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        THEN orders.subtotal
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) / NULLIF(
      SUM(
        CASE
          WHEN orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2025-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
          AND orders.ordered_at < CAST('2025-10-30 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
          THEN orders.subtotal
          ELSE 0
        END
      ),
      0
    ) - 1 AS "orders.growth"
  FROM orders AS orders
  WHERE
    orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2025-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
), _cm_orders__iif_ordered_at_2025_01_01_00_6195222a_btotal_0_sum AS (

      CASE
        WHEN orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2025-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        AND orders.ordered_at < CAST('2025-10-30 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        AND stores.opened_at < CAST('2025-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        THEN orders.subtotal
        ELSE 0
      END
    ) AS "orders.iif_ordered_at_2025_01_01_00_6195222a_btotal_0_sum"
  FROM orders AS orders
  LEFT JOIN stores AS stores
    ON orders.store_id = stores.id
  WHERE
    orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2025-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
), _cm_orders__iif_ordered_at_2026_01_01_00_24a87f15_btotal_0_sum AS (
  SELECT
    SUM(

        WHEN orders.ordered_at >= CAST('2026-01-01 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)
        AND orders.ordered_at < CAST('2026-10-30 00:00:00' AS TIMESTAMP)

args.message:
Year to date, revenue grew about 32.0% ($3,452,838 → $4,556,849). For the comparable stores alone it grew only about 7.4% ($3,299,245 → $3,543,155). So most of the headline growth comes from New Orleans, which opened in May 2025, and Los Angeles, which opened in November 2025.

How these were calculated:
- Revenue means pre-tax net sales, which is how the existing store-revenue examples define it.
- The last order in the data is on 2026-10-29, so both periods run from Jan 1 to Oct 29 inclusive, in 2026 and in 2025.
- Comparable stores are those that opened before 2025-01-01: Philadelphia, Brooklyn, Chicago and San Francisco.
